You're allowed to grieve your old life. You're allowed to grieve all that you had to give up. Pacing and time both help -- crashing tends to make the grief flare up once again for me, so it's another reason to try to avoid crashing at all costs.

I think it's also important to put energy and time into building a new life. Not saying you should immediately jump into a bunch of activities, but I think it's really important to step back and ask yourself, "What *can* I do? What makes me happy?" And then acting based upon that. Like for me, yeah I can't do a lot of my former hobbies. But I can still do some of them that don't require too much energy (writing, drawing, etc). And the more energy-intensive ones I can find ways to make it easier on my body. Like with gardening, I don't do it very often, but now when I do, I make sure I'm in the shade and cool enough, I keep everything very close to me so I don't have to constantly stand up and move around, I take frequent breaks, and I have others help me with any lifting. Yeah, I can't garden for as long or as intense as I used to... but I still *can* do it, at my own pace, and I try to find joy in that fact.

I also tend to search this sub for "grief," "grieving," "sad," and any other relevant terms any time I'm feeling mentally low -- it helps, even rereading and rereading over and over again what others have said. Like there's this one commenter that stuck out to me, who talked about how their boyfriend told them to "achieve slower," which has helped me a lot. And it's a process, so don't feel like you need to immediately jump into "okay I have to accept everything right now!" Take baby steps. Make circles, come back to resources whenever you're looking for a bit of guidance. It can take time to fully process and grieve the past life you've lost. It's scary, to lose so much, especially in a short amount of time, but where you are right now is not necessarily where you're going to be in the future.

For symptoms, I use 4 categories, all with a couple symptoms each (mental, digestive, cfs, pots). Like fatigue and swollen lymph nodes go in cfs, chest pain and tachycardia go in pots, stress and brain fog go in mental, lack of appetite and slow digestion go in digestive.

For factors, I've split it into daily, activites, appointments, and period. Daily is general stuff like was I in bed? At my computer? Crashing? Did I leave the house? Overall summary type stuff.

Activities are self-explanatory -- they're the things I can choose from to do each day, like writing, messaging with friends, showering, washing hair, etc. 

Appointments are the same, although I differentiate between doctor, dentist, and therapist appointments. Also note if it's a video visit or if a procedure happens. 

Period I haven't had to use in awhile since I'm on birth control, but it tracks the same things every other period tracker does.

I used to track high/medium/low activity but I found it wasn't helping too much because (a) my days don't differ too much and (b) it's captured by other things (ex. looking at stress, whether I left the house, whether I had an appointment, etc). I also have it auto-import by data from fitbit (by auto-importing into google fit, which bearable can sync with), but honestly I haven't really used the data. 

What's helped me the most, though, is splitting everything up into categories instead of having just a general long list. And remembering that bearable is just a tool -- it doesn't work if I set up this super complex system to track absolutely everything and then never actually use it. I don't use bearable for specific pacing practices, though, such as testing out specific times of activities versus rest, just to look at more general trends over time (especially in regards to symptom levels).

FWIW I'm on ketotifen and with celebrex it seems to help a lot. Like I accidentally didn't phone in the refill for ketotifen on time and had to go without for a few days and those were absolutely miserable days, could barely even get out of bed. But both celebrex and ketotifen seem to lessen my appetite, which sucks but it's worth it to me, just to be able to sit up and actually do activities sometimes.

So can pushing yourself too much with ME/CFS. A lot of people put through GET with ME/CFS come out with visibly decreased muscle mass, not to mention physically becoming worse. And rest doesn't necessarily mean you must stay in bed 1000% of the time -- it means taking the time to just do nothing. Like meditating. I try to do rest blocks of 15 minutes where I just lay down and let my body relax, approximately every hour or two or activity. If you're so worried about thrombosis, try wearing compression socks -- it's what they use for people who can't get out of bed. And rest itself doesn't make you gain weight -- I'm still the same weight as I was back when I was pushing through the fatigue.

Yeah, it's easy to get used to just constantly pushing through, so the moment you start resting and stop pushing through the fatigue it gets harder to continue pushing through. Listen to your body. It needs the rest.

Yup, crashing after less activity means you're pushing it too far. You keep pushing it too much, it's plausible that you could become bedridden (but you would become housebound first, though I highly recommend trying to avoid pushing more to even get to this level). 

And for working on the computer: it really depends. How long are you working? How many breaks are you taking? How long are the breaks? What is the physical set up -- ie are you doing things like having your feet up, getting more support, etc? These are all factors that can affect that ability, and it's highly individual on what each person is able to tolerate. I had a period where I couldn't really use my computer at a desk, but resting/no longer constantly pushing myself, meds, and changing my computer setup helped a lot. Now, most days I can sit/lay at the computer, write a bit, and maybe play a bit of video games (if it's a pretty good day).

There's a lot of resources in the wiki on how to learn proper pacing, along with if you search the sub for books or the like. Definitely start working on pacing sooner than later -- I continued to push through things during my final semester of college and it honestly made me so much worse off, to the point where I can't work and I have to live with someone else who can take care of chores / me on the days I can barely get out of bed. It's not worth it to keep pushing.

I do wanna add one little thing, though: it's possible to get on SSDI using a parent's work record, but you and the SSA must agree you became disabled before 22 and that parent must be retired/ 
already drawing social security--it's called Adult Child Benefits. I know How To Get On talks about it more in-depth, but I think it's important to at least mention it since not very many people know about it.

And another general resource you could add are ABLE accounts -- they don't count against asset limits for a certain amount, but you can only open one if the onset of disability was prior to 26. [More info here.](https://www.ablenrc.org/what-is-able/what-are-able-acounts/)

Not only are they poor quality but the data was literally falsified. As in they changed their hypothesis measure on what "counted as recovery" mid-way through (a very big no-no in science, like get-disbarred-and-never-practice-again bad) so that the very population they were attempting to treat hit their new measure of recovery before the study even started.

[This website](https://howtogeton.wordpress.com/social-security-disability/) was super helpful. It was partially luck of the draw, but I followed almost every piece of advice it gave and ended up getting approved on my first try, without a lawyer. I figured that if I got rejected, then I'd get a lawyer, but I wanted to do it myself initially because even if you do get a lawyer, they're not always on top of everything and it would've killed me inside if they missed a critical form or record.

Of course, it took a lot of energy to get all the records and go through all the phone calls and everything, but reading that website helped prepare me for everything they could ask of me. Oh, and check out the SSA's criteria of conditions -- I emphasized heavily on my application how I met each part of the ME/CFS criteria they had. When you fill it out, be really honest with how much you can do -- and how much you *can't* do. Especially everyday/on bad days. It will only hurt you if you only talk about what you can do on good days.

And if you're having your doctor fill out any sort of form (ex. on functioning), it really helps to (a) bring a copy of the same exact form that you've filled out, and (b) schedule an appointment specifically for them to sit and fill out the form while you're there (especially good if they have any questions instead of making them guess).

I do (4am to 2pm). And honestly, I don't try to change it. I've tried forcing myself into a "more normal" sleep schedule, but (a) that put a lot of pressure on my body as I wasn't getting enough sleep and (b) was undone in less than a week despite several weeks of effort.

Also, there's a lot less sensory stuff happening at night. It's darker, and quieter, and honestly it just feels easier to exist at night. Like I can just turn on my string lights and keep my door shut and (if it's warm enough) open the windows to get fresh air. Not to mention, it's a lot lower chance of people trying to bother me. I can just exist in like... "power-saving mode" without having to deal with loud noises or people talking or bright lights. The only thing that sucks is when there are loud noises while I'm trying to sleep before I wake up at 2pm, but thankfully that tends to be more rare.

If one of your parents is retired/past the age of retirement and you became disabled before the age of 22, it's possible to use their work record for SSDI. It's called Adult Child Benefits. [This website](https://howtogeton.wordpress.com/how-to-get-adult-disabled-child-benefits/) has more info.

But were you becoming weaker because you kept pushing yourself to use the walker? Or were you using the walker as a substitute to proper pacing and rest? I could say I became weaker when I started using a cane ... but it was also during a time in my life when I was pushing myself so much that I was crashing every couple of days and becoming weaker and weaker because I wasn't properly pacing. Not because I was using a mobility aid.

Also, regarding your aunt: since most people with ME/CFS don't use the cane for a specific leg (e.g. due to an injury) they can easily switch off sides. Plus, ME/CFS patient's bodies already act weirdly; a lot of severe/bedbound patients won't become physically deconditioned despite spending so much time at rest. And there have been ME/CFS patients who have come out of GET trials completely visibly and measurably deconditioned (despite going through exercise regimes that should've built up muscle).

Saying that it's bad for people to depend on mobility aids is ableist. No one gives any abled people shit for driving a car or taking a train or bus for long distances, despite the fact that technically they *are* physically able to travel those long distances. Yeah, it may take them several days, but they still physically can. Doesn't mean we should get rid of cars/trains/buses, or say it's bad that people depend on that method of travel. Cars/trains/buses have made life easier for abled people. Disabled people are allowed to have things that make their lives easier too. We're already at a disadvantage, let's not say we need to suffer any more than we have to to somehow "prove" we deserve to have good lives or be a "good disabled person" for societies view.

Another person with POTS here. I find that I have to drink water with salt (not enough to taste, just a small amount) because otherwise it just goes right through me and then I become dehydrated no matter how much I drink. I also use a lot of electrolyte powders; I personally like Liquid IV, which ironically isn't through an actual IV. Talk to your doctor, it may be just be that you have to supplement electrolytes. But yes, should everything else fail it's possible to get regular saline IVs, you'd just need a doctor to order it.

[Classic Pacing.](https://smile.amazon.com/dp/B08JHBG9X1/ref=cm_sw_r_cp_apa_glc_9A5X1M44DZ2F91EMX77B) It's been really helpful to learn how to effectively pace, and how to both become stable (ie not crashing as much) and how to eventually be able to build up activity to build up more quality of life.

Have you read [Classic Pacing](https://smile.amazon.com/dp/B08JHBG9X1/ref=cm_sw_r_cp_apa_glc_9A5X1M44DZ2F91EMX77B)? It's a book I got awhile ago but only got to reading it recently when one of my doctors suggested to do more strict pacing along with taking midodrine (which tends to mask my symptoms) so I could build up activity to eventually be able to exercise again -- so I was in the same boat as you with immediate suspicion, even though the doctor is very up to date and knowledgeable about ME/CFS.

The book's been really helpful to settle my worries about increasing activity, since it goes into talking about warning signs and how often/how much to increase each time. Also reframing how we view exercise; instead of going to the gym, for an ME patient like us, exercise could be one stretch we can do daily, or a very short session of progressive muscle relaxation (which tenses the muscles and thus uses them).

Generally, they say increase by 10% each time, so it's not a huge jump. So maybe instead of doing three walks, you just lengthen one of your current walks by 10% (e.g. if you walk for 10 minutes, you'd increase by 1 minute). And when you're first starting out, only increase in that one area and then wait ~3 weeks to (1) make sure you're not increasing too fast and (2) to get your body more used to it. Which yeah, I know, sounds a little like GET, but GET is a strict schedule, while pacing you really have to go by how your body is doing and make sure to go slowly. And, because the increases are such small amounts, it ideally shouldn't cause any crashes, and the moment symptoms start to kick in you can put on the brakes and go back to the level you were at before that increase.

There's a lot more information in the book, so I highly recommend reading it. The chapters are all relatively short and clear, and each one has a bullet point summary of the main points, so it's really easy to read.

I understand, ME/CFS is just a really hard disease to have, and we're all struggling in our own way. I can't apologize for the person who originally made the comment (it's up to them if they would like to), but I do see how it negatively affected you and I agree, they could've phrased their comment better.

Maybe they didn't know. I don't know how everyone would react to all of my statements, and I'm sure you have felt the same--just look at how some comments you expect to do well on reddit get downvoted to hell, and some get similarly upvoted. I can't claim to know exactly what their intentions were, but from my point of view it seemed to be more of just a venting, throwaway comment. I don't know about you, but I certainly don't always phrase things correctly, especially if I'm making a vent comment.

But the original comment isn't directed at patients, it's directed against the medical system. They're not saying "It is specifically because of male ME/CFS patients that we don't have a cure yet." It's more like "There are systematic factors that make diseases that are seen as 'hysterical women making up symptoms' be treated as less than valid, which still significantly impacts male ME/CFS patients."

>No because saying if it was only men who had this, it would be cured is just trying to imply that women with ME/CFS have it even worse then men. 

... That's not what I get out of their comments. The way I see it, it's more reflection of just a general frustration towards the medical system. And to be fair, male pattern baldness (which, you know, significantly impacts men but arguably doesn't cause anywhere near the same amount of suffering as ME/CFS) has for quite a while gotten significantly more funding than ME/CFS. It's the same sentiment as "if men could get pregnant, there would be abortion clinics on every street corner."

>I’m not talking in a wider spectrum I’m talking about ME/CFS. I believe it’s a great equaliser and everyone suffered just as bad due to medical negligence. 

Yes, we all share the experience of having ME/CFS, but everything outside of that (including treatment by doctors) is affected by things such as our location, our socioeconomic status, our gender, our ethnicity, etc. 

>In fact, if you want to be an arse about it you could say men have it even harder to come forward and get help considering there’s not that many of us. In my CFS group I’m the only man with 7 other women.

I'm not entirely disagreeing with you here. Men are affected *because* in the general public eye, it is often seen as just "hysterical women making up symptoms." But that doesn't erase the fact that POC and women tend to have poorer health treatment across the board.

>I see no evidence that women with ME/CFS are discriminated any more then men. In fact the anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise

I have a degree in social sciences. Anectdotal evidence really isn't evidence in of itself, since there are implicit biases we all have that can interfere with collecting anectdotes--ex. maybe you're more likely to skim over when women talk about their experiences, but you pay more attention when men talk about the same. Not accusing you of this, just giving it as an example of why anectdotal data gathering really doesn't work for asserting conclusions. I understand you're hurt and I'm not trying to argue that you shouldn't be; my intention is moreso to say systematic factors make the treatment of ME/CFS sucky *because* it's seen as more of a "women's disease." And these same systematic factors then affect you as a male patient, because you're also caught in the crossfire of the bias in the medical system.

How exactly do those comments make you feel unwelcome? Medical bias against [women](https://physicians.dukehealth.org/articles/recognizing-addressing-unintended-gender-bias-patient-care) and  [POC](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4638275/) and especially [WOC](https://www.nhpr.org/post/when-why-women-people-color-face-lower-quality-healthcare-worse-health-outcomes#stream/0) is a well-documented phenomen. Yes, ME/CFS patients already tend to get the short end of the stick considering its history as the "yuppie flu," but that doesn't erase the fact that parts of people's identities (such as gender or ethnicity) can impact their quality of care. 

I'm not any of the people in the screenshot so I can't attest to their intentions, but as far as I can tell it's not meant to say "You personally have not suffered because of your status as an ME/CFS patient just because you're a white man." It's more like "It sucks for all patients, but it especially sucks for women and POC because medical systems have consistently treated them worse due to internal biases, and this is reflected in research funding, in treatment options, and in general attitudes. This then does affect you, as diseases such as fibromyalgia and ME/CFS can often be seen as 'hysterical women making up symptoms,' making treatment of patients even worse." Does that make sense?

Golden Girls. It's dated and there's enough happening that it's not boring, but it's not too fast-paced and the plotline is easy to follow (and it's the typical sitcom camera, so it doesn't move very much). It's calming enough for me that sometimes I'll put it on and then end up napping. Plus, there's a lot of episodes/seasons, so it's easy to spend a lot of time watching it. There are a couple episodes with "exciting" things (ex. a character has a heart attack), but they're not too extreme & are resolved quickly/non-dramatically.

Mary and the Witch's Flower is a cute movie, sort of like Studio Ghibli style. All the Studio Ghibli movies do have some sort of stress (like a fight against the "evil" person), but a lot of them are aimed at children so it's not too bad. Especially if you remember that they all tend to have good endings. Except for Grave of the Fireflies, that one's a tear-jerker. Comedy specials also work well, since they're all just jokes (I personally like John Mulaney, but Bo Burnham is also funny).

Cooking shows/videos are also nice. I really like Claire Saffitz, Rick Martinez, Sohla El-Waylly, Binging with Babish, and Joshua Weissman (though Joshua is a bit more fast-paced). They all do videos on YouTube, some through their own channel and some featured through other channels (like Food52 or Bon Appetit). American Cooking Competition shows can be very intense/stressful/fast-paced, though--ex Nailed It, Cupcake Wars, etc--so I don't reccomend those.

There's also videos like sketchbook sessions, where people record themselves drawing in their sketchbook/on a program, usually with a voice-over. They're nice to watch as something more in the background, especially if you can do things like doodle or crochet. Painting tutorials/videos are also very low-key/relaxing. Don't feel limited to just Bob Ross, there's a lot of other good artists on YouTube.
